nodes.label: Multimedia Learning Principles
nodes.one_line: Apply Mayer's principles (coherence, signaling, redundancy) so added media reduces cognitive load instead of competing for it.
know_what: Coherence principle — exclude extraneous words, pictures, and sounds that don't support the instructional goal, even when they're engaging
Signaling principle — use cues such as arrows, highlighting, or headings to draw attention to essential material within a display
Redundancy principle — avoid presenting identical text and narration simultaneously, since reading and listening to the same words competes for the same channel
Spatial contiguity principle — place printed words near the corresponding part of a graphic rather than separated on the page or screen
Temporal contiguity principle — present corresponding narration and animation at the same time rather than sequentially
Modality principle — present words as narration alongside a graphic rather than as on-screen text alongside the same graphic, freeing the visual channel
know_how: Cut a decorative image, sound effect, or tangent that doesn't support the instructional goal, even if it makes the slide more engaging
Add a signaling cue, such as an arrow, bold text, or a callout, to direct attention to the one element in a busy display that matters most
Replace simultaneous identical on-screen text and narration with narration alone plus a supporting visual
Move a text label physically next to the part of a diagram it describes instead of into a separate legend
Synchronize narration timing with the animation or diagram it describes, instead of narrating before or after the visual changes
Choose narration over on-screen text for explanatory content that pairs with a graphic, reserving on-screen text for technical terms or non-native-language support
habits: Ask what instructional goal a decorative element serves before keeping it
Read a slide's text and listen to its narration separately to check for word-for-word redundancy
Check that a diagram's labels sit next to what they're labeling
Notice when narration and the visual it describes are out of sync
Prefer narration paired with a graphic over on-screen text paired with the same graphic, for explanatory content

know_why.claim: Interesting but instructionally irrelevant details, such as an engaging photo or an entertaining anecdote, should be cut from learning material even when they increase interest.
know_why.because: seductive-details research shows irrelevant-but-interesting material reliably harms retention of the actual content by diverting limited attention
know_why.disputed_by: practitioners focused on motivation and completion, who argue that in low-stakes or voluntary contexts a small engagement cost is worth the retention tradeoff if it keeps learners from dropping out before finishing the material at all
know_why.source: Mayer and colleagues, coherence principle and seductive-details research, vs. motivational-design practitioners such as Keller's ARCS model prioritizing sustained attention

nodes.checkpoint: Redesign one existing slide or screen against the coherence, signaling, redundancy, and spatial/temporal contiguity principles, and identify at least one specific element removed or moved.
nodes.common_failure: Adding narration that reads the on-screen text word for word, which research shows actively hurts retention compared to either channel alone, despite feeling thorough.
sources: Mayer & Moreno, cognitive theory of multimedia learning
Ruth Clark & Richard Mayer, e-Learning and the Science of Instruction

nodes.label: Accessible Media Production
nodes.one_line: Produce media that's usable without sight, hearing, or a mouse, built in from the start instead of retrofitted.
know_what: WCAG success criteria — the specific, testable rules covering contrast ratio, keyboard operability, and text alternatives that define what 'accessible' means in practice, not just the general principle
Alt text — a text alternative for an image conveyed to screen-reader users, written to communicate the image's instructional purpose, not just describe its contents literally
Closed captions vs. open captions — captions a viewer can toggle off versus captions burned permanently into the video, each appropriate to different distribution contexts
Color contrast ratio — the minimum luminance difference between text and background, commonly 4.5:1 for normal text under WCAG AA, required for readability by low-vision users
Keyboard operability — every interactive element reachable and operable without a mouse, a requirement for users with motor impairments and many screen-reader users
Transcript — a full text version of audio or video content, useful for deaf users, non-native speakers, and anyone who can't play audio in their current environment
know_how: Write alt text that conveys an image's instructional purpose in context, rather than a generic literal description or leaving it blank
Check color contrast against WCAG AA thresholds using a contrast-checking tool before finalizing a color palette
Add accurate closed captions to every video, synced to the audio, not auto-generated captions left uncorrected
Test every interactive screen using only a keyboard, confirming every action a mouse user could take is also reachable by tab and enter
Provide a full transcript for any audio-only content, such as podcasts or narration-only segments
Run an accessibility checker, built into most authoring tools, as a build step, not a separate audit weeks after launch
habits: Write alt text for what an image is doing instructionally, not just what it shows
Tab through a new interactive screen with the mouse unplugged before calling it done
Correct auto-generated captions instead of shipping them uncorrected
Check contrast ratios during design, not after a stakeholder or user flags a problem
Provide a transcript for any audio-only content by default, not only when a learner requests one
nodes.checkpoint: Produce one media asset, a video or interactive screen, that passes a WCAG AA contrast check, has accurate captions or a transcript, and is fully operable using only a keyboard.
nodes.common_failure: Treating accessibility as a final compliance pass done by someone else after content is built, so structural problems such as color choices or missing keyboard paths require expensive rework instead of being avoided in the first draft.
sources: WebAIM accessibility guidance and contrast checker

nodes.label: Authoring Tool Fluency
nodes.one_line: Build interactive e-learning content in an authoring tool (Articulate, Rise, H5P) without hand-coding around its limits.
know_what: Authoring tool — software such as Articulate Storyline, Rise, Adobe Captivate, or H5P, purpose-built to produce interactive e-learning without general programming
SCORM / xAPI — the packaging and tracking standards authoring tools export to, determining what an LMS can actually record about a learner's interaction

Slide-based vs. responsive-block authoring — a distinction between tools built around fixed-layout slides, such as Storyline, and tools built around reflowing content blocks, such as Rise, each with different tradeoffs for custom interactivity versus mobile responsiveness
Master slide / template — a reusable layout and style definition that keeps a course visually consistent without manually reformatting every screen
Variable and trigger logic — the tool's mechanism for building conditional behavior, such as showing specific feedback based on a selected answer, without code
Publish and test cycle — the process of publishing a build, testing it in a real LMS or browser context, and catching platform-specific bugs before final delivery
know_how: Build a course section using master slides or templates so visual consistency doesn't require manually reformatting every screen
Set up variables and triggers to build a conditional interaction, such as branching feedback or a knowledge check gating progress, without writing code
Choose between a slide-based and a responsive-block tool based on whether the project needs custom interactivity or true mobile responsiveness
Publish a build to SCORM or xAPI and test it inside a real LMS or a SCORM test player, not just inside the authoring tool's preview
Diagnose a common publish-time bug, such as a tracking issue, a broken trigger, or a font substitution, using the tool's known troubleshooting steps
Keep a source file organized, with named slides and grouped layers, so another team member could pick up the build without reverse-engineering it
habits: Test a build in the actual target LMS, not just the authoring tool's internal preview
Use master slides and templates from the start instead of retrofitting consistency later
Name and organize the source file as if someone else will need to open it
Check that a trigger or variable actually fires as intended, not just that it compiles without an error
Publish and re-test after every significant change instead of assuming the last successful test still holds
nodes.checkpoint: Build a short interactive module in an authoring tool using at least one master template, one conditional trigger, and a published SCORM or xAPI package that tracks correctly in a real LMS.
nodes.common_failure: Building an entire course as one-off custom slides with no template, so a late brand or layout change requires manually editing every single screen instead of updating one master.
sources: SCORM.com, SCORM and xAPI standards guidance

nodes.label: Interactivity Design
nodes.one_line: Design an interaction that requires a real decision from the learner, not a click-to-continue disguised as engagement.
know_what: Meaningful interactivity — an interaction requiring a decision relevant to the objective, as opposed to clicking to proceed
Branching scenario — a decision-point structure where a learner's choice changes what they see next, used to practice judgment under realistic consequences
Gating vs. free navigation — restricting progress until a step is completed versus letting a learner move freely, a tradeoff between control and learner autonomy
Feedback specificity — feedback that explains why an answer was right or wrong, tied to the underlying concept, rather than just marking correct or incorrect
Interaction pattern library — a set of proven, reusable interaction types, such as scenario, sorting, drag-classification, or simulation, chosen for fit to the objective rather than novelty
Cognitive cost of interactivity — every interaction has a cost in learner time and attention, which must be justified by what it teaches, not just by making a screen feel less static
know_how: Design a branching scenario with at least two meaningfully different consequence paths, not a single 'right answer, try again' loop
Write feedback that explains the underlying reasoning for a wrong answer, not just 'incorrect, try again'
Decide whether to gate progress or allow free navigation based on whether the sequence has a genuine dependency, not by default
Select an interaction pattern from what's proven to fit the objective's cognitive demand, resisting the pull toward a novel interaction that doesn't add instructional value
Estimate the time cost of a planned interaction against what it actually teaches before committing production budget to it
Pilot a branching scenario's paths to confirm every path is reachable and none dead-ends without resolution
habits: Ask what decision this interaction requires the learner to make
Write feedback that teaches the concept, not just the verdict
Question a gate that exists out of habit rather than a real dependency
Trace every branch in a scenario to confirm it resolves, before calling it finished
Check whether an interaction is justified by what it teaches, not just by making a screen feel less static
nodes.checkpoint: Design a branching scenario with at least three decision points and two distinct consequence paths, with feedback at each point explaining the underlying reasoning, and confirm every branch resolves.
nodes.common_failure: Building an interaction that looks sophisticated, such as drag-and-drop or animated branching, but reduces to a single correct path with generic 'try again' feedback, adding production cost without adding instructional value.
sources: Cathy Moore, Action Mapping scenario-based design
Clark Aldrich, simulation and scenario design
Michael Allen, Michael Allen's Guide to E-Learning

nodes.label: Video & Screencast Production
nodes.one_line: Script, record, and edit instructional video short enough and clear enough that learners actually finish it.
know_what: Script — a written, timed document specifying every line of narration and corresponding visual, reviewed and approved before recording starts
Screencast — a recorded capture of a screen, such as a software demo or workflow walkthrough, typically requiring a clean environment and rehearsed pacing rather than live improvisation

Chunked video length — instructional video retention drops sharply past a well-documented length threshold, commonly cited around six minutes for online video, arguing for multiple short videos over one long one
B-roll and cutaways — supplementary footage used to maintain visual interest and illustrate a concept without requiring the primary subject to be on screen the whole time
Audio quality floor — the minimum microphone and room-noise standard below which viewers disengage regardless of content quality, often a more common failure point than video quality
Editing pass structure — a defined sequence, such as rough cut, narration sync, graphics or caption pass, and final review, that keeps production organized instead of one continuous edit session
know_how: Write and get sign-off on a timed script before recording, specifying narration and corresponding visuals line by line
Break a long topic into multiple short videos at natural conceptual boundaries rather than one long continuous recording
Record with a dedicated microphone and a quiet, treated space, prioritizing audio quality over video production value
Rehearse a screencast recording at least once to fix pacing and eliminate dead air before the final take
Add captions and check them against the transcript for accuracy, not just auto-generated placement
Run a structured editing pass, rough cut, narration sync, graphics, final review, instead of one continuous unstructured edit
habits: Script and approve before recording, not the reverse
Check audio quality first when a draft video feels off, before assuming the problem is visual
Cut a long recording into shorter, single-concept videos at natural breaks
Watch a finished video start to finish once before calling it done, not just spot-check clips
Get script sign-off from the SME or sponsor before recording, to avoid re-recording after the fact
nodes.checkpoint: Script, record, and edit a single-concept instructional video under six minutes with accurate captions, clean audio, and a structured editing pass documented in stages.
nodes.common_failure: Recording a long, unscripted screencast in one take and publishing it with minor trims, producing a video with dead air, rambling explanation, and a length that guarantees most learners drop off before the end.
sources: Cathy Moore, video for learning guidance
Ruth Clark & Richard Mayer, e-Learning and the Science of Instruction

nodes.label: Production Review & QA
nodes.one_line: Catch the broken link, mistimed caption, and off-brand asset before a learner does.
know_what: QA pass types — functional (does every button and trigger work), content (does it match the approved storyboard), and technical (does it run correctly on target devices, browsers, and the LMS)
Cross-browser / cross-device testing — checking a build on the actual range of browsers, devices, and screen sizes the audience will use, not just the developer's own setup
QA checklist — a standardized, reusable list of things to check on every build, so review quality doesn't depend on one reviewer's memory
Broken-link and dead-trigger audit — a specific, common category of e-learning defect, such as a button that goes nowhere or a link to a removed page, that's easy to miss without a systematic pass
Regression — a defect introduced by a later fix that breaks something that previously worked, which argues for retesting beyond just the specific change made
Sign-off record — a documented approval, with reviewer name and date, that a build passed QA before it's released, protecting against 'I thought someone checked that'
know_how: Run a QA pass using a standardized checklist covering functional, content, and technical categories, not an unstructured click-through
Test a build across the actual range of target browsers, devices, and screen sizes rather than only the developer's own setup
Audit every link, button, and trigger systematically for dead ends or mismatched destinations
Compare the built content against the approved storyboard line by line to catch content drift introduced during build
Retest around a bug fix for regressions, not just the specific defect that was fixed
Record sign-off with reviewer name and date before a build is marked ready for release
habits: Use the checklist every time, even on a build that looks obviously fine
Test on a device or browser you don't personally use, not just your own setup
Click every interactive element at least once, not just the ones on the happy path
Retest around any late fix instead of assuming it only touched what it was meant to touch
Keep a signed-off defect log for every release, not just a mental note that it looked fine
nodes.checkpoint: Run a full QA pass on a built module using a standardized checklist across functional, content, and technical categories, across at least two different browsers or devices, and produce a signed-off defect log.
nodes.common_failure: QA-ing only the happy path a designer expects learners to take, missing the broken link or dead trigger on a less obvious path that a real learner finds within the first week of launch.
sources: ATD QA and production review guidance
ISTQB software testing fundamentals, adapted for e-learning QA
Articulate / Rise publishing and testing documentation
